In the incubator's meeting room, Disha read the survey scores aloud. "Weak. People said nice list and never came back."

Ritu had built a tool-sharing app for her colony whose first version only listed who owned what. She looked at the results for a long while. "Nobody could ask for a drill. That was the whole point." She opened her laptop and added one button: Borrow tonight. Then she set up two-week cycles: release on Monday, watch what forty residents actually tap for ten days, meet on the second Friday and change something.

In the first cycle, most taps landed on drills and ladders, and almost nobody opened the profile page. Ritu deleted the profile page and moved ladders to the top.

Disha nodded. "That's evidence, not opinion."

qa.q: What could Ritu do if taps stay low even after adding the button?
qa.a: Ritu could talk to a few residents about why they do not borrow, then change the next cycle's version to match.

qa.a: Disha may be impressed that Ritu responds to what people do, as "That's evidence, not opinion" suggests.

Dear Ojas,
Thank you for testing the first version of the tuition-finder app last month. Your honest feedback, "I don't see why I'd use this," stung, but you were right.
I went back to why I started. Parents in our colony don't just want a list of tutors. They want to know which tutors other parents trust. That was the whole idea, and I'd left it out to launch faster.
So I added one thing: short reviews from parents whose children have studied with each tutor. Nothing else.
Since then I've been working in two-week cycles. At the end of each, I look at what people actually did, not what they said. In the first cycle, most people read reviews but never messaged a tutor. So I added a "call" button. Messages doubled in the second cycle.
Would you try it again?
Vinita

qa.q: What one thing did Vinita add after the first feedback?
qa.a: Short reviews from parents whose children have studied with each tutor.

qa.q: How did Vinita feel reading Ojas's feedback?
qa.a: Vinita felt stung, but also saw that Ojas was right.

qa.q: Why is looking at what people did better than only asking what they think?
qa.a: Because actions show real use, like reading reviews but not messaging, which led to the call button that doubled messages.

qa.q: How might Ojas feel being asked to try it again?
qa.a: Ojas may feel respected and curious, seeing that the honest feedback led to real changes.

grounding: It shows a founder who, after weak feedback, adds the one feature that makes the idea worthwhile and runs two-week cycles based on what users actually do.

Ganga, you asked on the show how our library-sharing app survived its first flop. So here's Aadhya's honest version.
Our first release was just a list of books people owned. Nobody used it. The feedback was polite and useless: "Nice idea," "Looks clean."
I sat with my co-founder and asked, why did we start this? Because people in apartment buildings have shelves full of books they've read once, and neighbours who'd love to borrow them. The magic was the borrowing, and the first version didn't even let you ask to borrow.
So we added one button: "Ask to borrow." Then we worked in two-week sprints. At the end of each, we looked only at what people did. First sprint, people asked but never returned books. So we added a gentle return reminder. Second sprint, returns went up.
We stopped guessing, and started watching.

qa.q: What button did Aadhya's team add?
How did Aadhya feel about the first feedback?
qa.a: Aadhya found it polite but useless, and seemed frustrated that it gave no real direction.

qa.q: What else could Aadhya's team look at in the next sprint?
qa.a: They could check which buildings borrow the most and learn why, so other buildings can be helped to do the same.

qa.q: How might the neighbours using the app experience the new version?
qa.a: They can finally ask to borrow and get gentle reminders to return books, so sharing feels easy and fair.

grounding: It shows a founder who adds the one feature that made the idea worthwhile after weak feedback, then runs two-week cycles based on what users do.
